query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Sliding-induced dynamic amorphization in HEA protective coatings creates an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer that triggers inverse Hall–Petch effects, thereby reducing friction and enhancing wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a coarse-grained, homogeneous microstructure in its as-deposited state.
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to a controlled sliding wear test designed to trigger dynamic amorphization (by varying load or sliding speed) while maintaining an inert environment to minimize oxidation.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under inert (ultra-high vacuum) or low-oxidation conditions and sliding speeds/loads within the regime that has been shown to induce dynamic amorphization without causing excessive thermal degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer via sliding-induced dynamic amorphization.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, localized stress and shear initiate amorphization at the surface, which then rapidly recrystallizes into an ultra-nanocrystalline structure. The resulting grain refinement yields an inverse Hall–Petch effect, lowering the shear strength and friction coefficient while enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline samples with a coarse microstructure, the treated coatings will show a measurable reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate, concomitant with evidence (via TEM/STEM) of a refined, ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings that are not subjected to the controlled sliding conditions and retain their original coarse-grained microstructure, leading to higher friction and wear under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold over the range of sliding speeds, loads, and inert conditions where dynamic amorphization is activated; it may not be applicable in highly oxidative environments or under conditions that do not produce sufficient local stresses.
generation.uncertainty: The precise sliding parameters (e.g., critical load or velocity) that optimize dynamic amorphization remain to be defined, and the uniformity/extent of the nanocrystalline layer may vary with testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coating samples: one set subjected to the controlled sliding wear test designed to induce dynamic amorphization (test group) and another maintained under identical conditions without sufficient sliding force or speed (control group). Characterize the surface microstructure using TEM/STEM, record friction coefficients during sliding, and measure wear rates post-test.
measurements: Wear volume loss (using profilometry or mass loss)
XRD analysis for amorphous phase detection
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the test group does not develop a distinct ultra-nanocrystalline layer compared to the control, or if the friction coefficient and wear rates do not show significant improvement in the test group relative to the control, then the hypothesis that dynamic amorphization governs enhanced wear performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

reading.lever: Control sliding-induced dynamic amorphization to form an ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
reading.why: Because evidence from inverse Hall-Petch studies shows that transforming the surface microstructure under wear can directly lower friction and improve wear resistance in HEA coatings.
